title: Sagittarius B2 (NIRCam image)
caption: The Sagittarius B2 molecular cloud, imaged by the James Webb Space Telescope
credit: NASA, ESA, CSA, STScI, A. Ginsburg (University of Florida), N. Budaiev (University of Florida), T. Yoo (University of Florida). Image processing: A. Pagan (STScI)

recognition.text: Ranked #32 on ESA/Webb’s published “Top 100 Images” list (an institutional selection, not an audience score).

story: A wide field of stars, broken up by clumps of orange cloud, fills this view. It shows Sagittarius B2, a molecular cloud near the centre of our galaxy, as seen by Webb's Near-Infrared Camera. A molecular cloud is a cold, dense region of gas and dust, the kind of place where new stars can form.

In near-infrared light, stars, gas and dust in the cloud all glow. This particular kind of light shows more of the region's diverse, colourful stars, but less of the structure in its gas and dust than other views do.

That trade-off is why astronomers use more than one instrument. Each of Webb's instruments adds its own piece of information, and together they help build a fuller picture of what is going on in this part of the galactic centre. This near-infrared image is one part of that larger set of observations.

understand.summary: This is a near-infrared image from Webb's NIRCam using eleven filters. The shortest wavelengths are shown in blue, then cyan, green, yellow and orange, with the longest, including a carbon monoxide filter, in red.
understand.eye: Near-infrared light is invisible to the human eye, so the colours are assigned to reveal differences between stars and clouds.
